records.our_prose: Apricots are usually trained to an open-center or vase shape: three to four evenly spaced main branches (called scaffolds) from a short trunk, with an open middle. Apricot fruits on short spurs that live several years as well as on last year's wood, so it needs less hard pruning than a peach.

records.our_prose: Thin the little fruits so that about one apricot is left every 4 to 6 inches along each branch, picking off the extras while they are small. This one step does the most for fruit size, keeps branches from breaking, and helps the tree crop more evenly each year. It also lets you remove damaged fruit early.
records.source_context: Trees typically over-bear and will produce many small, less-useable fruits unless fruit is thinned. When fruits are grape-sized, thin to one fruit every 4 to 6 inches along the branch to increase size of remaining fruit and to maintain tree health.

records.our_prose: Chill is amply met in every zone here (this variety range needs 350 to 700 hours; the region banks far more), so the limiting factor is not cold, it is the cool, wet maritime spring. Apricot blooms earliest of any tree fruit grown here, and WSU's western Washington fruit handbook flags it as very sensitive to frost at bloom time; even where frost does not strike, cool, damp bloom-time weather keeps pollinators from working the flowers well and favors brown rot and coryneum blight on stone fruit generally. Reliable fruiting is genuinely site-dependent: the warmest, driest, most sheltered spot available, a late-blooming variety, and attentive dormant-season disease control are what turn a marginal crop into a real one.

records.source_context: Apricots Apricots (Prunus armeniaca) are difficult to grow in our conditions because they bloom early and are susceptible to many diseases. They are very sensitive to frost at bloom time and require sprays to control brown rot both at bloom and pre-harvest. Even when the trees are healthy they may produce a good crop only about one year in three.

records.our_prose: Plant the bare-root tree while it is still dormant (resting, no leaves) in late winter to early spring, before the buds open, once the ground can be dug; in mild-winter areas that means December through February. Soak the roots in a bucket for an hour or two first. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots without bending them, and set the tree so the graft union (the bumpy joint near the base, where the variety meets the rootstock) sits 2 to 3 inches above the soil. Do not put fertilizer in the hole. Refill with the same soil, water in well, and add a stake only if it is windy. Most of all, avoid low, frosty spots, because apricot blooms so early that late frosts are its biggest threat.

records.our_prose: Plant the bare-root tree while dormant in late winter to early spring, before bud break, once the ground can be worked; in mild-winter regions this is December through February. Soak the roots an hour or two beforehand. Dig a hole wide enough to spread the roots without bending them and set the tree with the graft union (the swollen joint near the base) 2 to 3 inches above the final soil line. Do not fertilize the hole; backfill with native soil, water in well, and stake if the site is windy. Above all, choose a planting spot that is not a frost pocket, since apricot's very early bloom is its greatest vulnerability.
